topic: Why Crossing a 230-Foot Swaying Bridge Made Strangers Mistake Fear for Chemistry
visual_mode_reason: Pairs North Vancouver's outdoor 230-foot swaying Capilano Suspension Bridge versus the 10-foot solid cedar bridge (R72/R79-M physical cable-grip & tear-off phone slip action) with 3D cyan MNI152 amygdala-insula heartbeat surge mislabeled by ventromedial prefrontal cortex (R78).
setup_18w: Researchers interviewed travelers crossing either a high swaying canyon bridge or a low sturdy cedar bridge.

primary_case.title: Donald G. Dutton & Arthur P. Aron's 1974 Capilano Canyon Suspension Bridge Misattribution-of-Arousal Studies
primary_case.place: Capilano Canyon Suspension Bridge, North Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada
primary_case.summary: In 1974 (Journal of Personality and Social Psychology), UBC psychologists Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron stationed interviewers on a swaying 230-foot canyon suspension bridge and a solid 10-foot upstream cedar bridge—showing a racing heartbeat quadrupled follow-up phone calls (50.0% vs 12.5%) until waiting 10 minutes on a park bench cut the effect in half.

people.role: University of British Columbia social psychologists (JPSP, 1974) who tested misattribution of autonomic arousal across two canyon bridges and park-bench cooldown controls

people.name: Hugo D. Critchley, Sarah N. Garfinkel & Lisa Feldman Barrett Team
people.role: Modern human interoception neuroscientists (Current Opinion in Psychology, 2017; Nature Human Behaviour, 2017) who mapped how the insula and prefrontal cortex interpret unlabelled visceral heartbeat signals

people.name: Cindy M. Meston, Craig A. Foster & Douglas T. Kenrick
people.role: Replication, meta-analysis, and boundary-condition researchers (1979–2003) clarifying when residual arousal amplifies attraction versus irritation

three_layer_formula.everyday_problem: Mistaking coffee jitters, turbulent travel, or work-deadline adrenaline for sudden interpersonal sparks—or picking an evening argument with your spouse simply because traffic left your pulse racing.

psychology_experiment.summary: Dutton & Aron (1974, JPSP) interviewed unaccompanied men crossing a swaying 230-foot suspension bridge versus a solid 10-foot cedar bridge, finding 50.0% (9/18) vs 12.5% (2/16) called the female interviewer afterward—and waiting 10 minutes past the bridge cut calls from 65% to 30%.

neuroscience_mechanism.summary: Kleckner, Barrett et al. (2017, Nature Human Behaviour) and Critchley & Garfinkel (2017) demonstrated that large-scale human interoceptive networks (amygdala, anterior insula, and ventromedial prefrontal cortex) receive raw visceral heartbeat and sweat signals without a built-in cause tag, constructing emotional meaning from the nearest salient social cue.

Foster, Witcher, Campbell & Green (1998, JPSP) quantitative synthesis of arousal-and-attraction experiments.

Critchley & Garfinkel (2017, Current Opinion in Psychology) neural model of cardiac interoception shaping social emotion.

core_facts.fact: In 1974 (Journal of Personality and Social Psychology), University of British Columbia psychologists Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron compared two bridges spanning North Vancouver's Capilano River: a 450-foot-long plank suspension bridge swaying 230 feet above rocky rapids versus a solid, non-swaying cedar bridge just 10 feet above a calm stream.

As unaccompanied men crossed either bridge, a female interviewer asked them to write a brief story about an ambiguous picture card and tore off the corner of a sheet with her name and phone number in case they wanted study details later (Dutton & Aron, 1974).

In Study 1 of Dutton and Aron (1974), 50.0% of travelers interviewed mid-span on the swaying 230-foot canyon bridge phoned the female interviewer afterward, compared with just 12.5% on the sturdy 10-foot cedar bridge—four times the callback rate!

When a male interviewer ran the exact same script on both bridges in Study 1 of Dutton and Aron (1974), callbacks stayed near floor on both spans (2 of 23 vs 1 of 22), proving cliffside fear did not simply make travelers eager to chat about psychology.

To rule out the loophole that thrill-seekers naturally flock to high bridges, Study 2 of Dutton and Aron (1974) tested men who ALL crossed the scary 230-foot bridge: 65% phoned when interviewed right on the swaying span, versus 30% when interviewed 10 minutes after crossing on a calm park bench once their pulse slowed.

Cindy Meston and Penny Frohlich (2003, Archives of Sexual Behavior) replicated excitation transfer at a real amusement park, finding unpartnered adults exiting a thrilling roller coaster rated photos of strangers significantly more attractive than riders waiting in line.

Douglas Kenrick, Robert Cialdini, and Darwyn Linder (1979, PSPB) and Craig Foster et al. (1998, JPSP) clarified a vital boundary: when people stay acutely locked onto an obvious source of fear—or when the person in front of them is unpleasant—arousal does not turn into attraction and can amplify irritation instead.

Human neuroimaging by Kleckner, Barrett, and colleagues (2017, Nature Human Behaviour) and Critchley and Garfinkel (2017) proved the anterior insula and amygdala deliver intense heartbeat signals without a printed return address—leaving ventromedial prefrontal networks to infer why your heart is pounding from surrounding social context.

wow_facts.fact: Same person, same clipboard, same torn paper phone slip: 12.5% called after meeting on a sturdy 10-foot creek bridge, while 50.0% called after meeting 230 feet above Capilano Gorge.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Your heartbeat carries no nametag—your brain guesses why your chest is thumping by looking at whoever is standing in front of you.

wow_facts.fact: In Study 2, simply waiting 10 minutes on a cedar park bench after crossing the scary bridge cut phone calls in half (from 65% down to 30%).
wow_facts.why_surprising: Proves daredevil personality wasn't the secret—ten minutes of pulse recovery changed romantic judgment in the exact same travelers.

wow_facts.fact: Adrenaline is an amplifier, not a blind love potion: Foster et al. (1998) showed leftover physical arousal makes warm people seem magnetic AND makes irritating situations feel twice as aggravating.
wow_facts.why_surprising: Explains both why adventure travel rekindles 20-year marriages and why rush-hour traffic sparks kitchen arguments at 6 PM.

misconceptions.myth: Only reckless thrill-seekers walk onto high suspension bridges, so personality—not brain misattribution—caused the 4x surge.
misconceptions.truth: Dutton and Aron's Study 2 tested travelers who ALL crossed the 230-foot bridge; letting their pulse cool for 10 minutes on a bench past the exit halved callbacks from 65% to 30%.

misconceptions.myth: Any scary situation automatically makes people fall for anyone nearby.
misconceptions.truth: Kenrick, Cialdini, and Linder (1979) and Foster et al. (1998) showed misattribution works strongest during lingering, ambiguous arousal paired with a pleasant person—and backfires if the target is annoying.

everyday_hooks: Walking through the front door after tense highway traffic with your pulse still high—and snapping over an unwashed coffee mug because your brain misreads lingering road adrenaline as domestic frustration.
Discovering why trying a slightly nerve-racking new hike, kayak paddle, or dance class together rekindles warmth in a 25-year marriage better than another quiet dinner.
Taking ten slow minutes to let coffee or work adrenaline settle before making a big personal call or relationship judgment.

debate_ignition.prebunk_myth: We trust a racing heartbeat as pure gut intuition about a person—forgetting our brain can't tell canyon adrenaline apart from real chemistry.
